demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

Maladaptive Strategies.value: perform mental rituals to prevent bad things from happening again
I remind myself it could have been worse
I dwell on what I have done wrong

Threat.value: I often react as if I am in danger even when nothing is actually wrong
I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people

Memory.value: When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory
I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns
When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.

Negative Appraisals.value: Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation
I feel isolated and set apart from others
The person I have become is unrecognisable to me

issues.item: Self-Harm Distraction: I hurt myself physically to stop thinking about the event
issues.explanation: Self-harm as a coping strategy is not impossible, but in this profile it is the only markedly high-risk/impulsive strategy and is poorly supported by the rest of the selected nodes. The other strategies are comparatively cognitive/obsessional (mental rituals, downward comparison), and the threat/memory/appraisal items do not show the broader dysregulation, dissociation, or severe affective overload that would make this combination clinically cohesive.

issues.item: Pain Recall: When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event
issues.explanation: Pain recall implies the patient was physically injured in the traumatic event. That is hard to reconcile with the trauma type 'accidentally caused serious injury to another' unless she was also injured, which is not otherwise reflected anywhere in the profile. The rest of the memory items emphasize fragmented retrieval and sensory reliving, but not a personally injured trauma narrative.

vignette: Amara stood on the concrete slab of the midtown commercial build when the secondary steel strut gave way. She had just finalized the drawings, confident in every beam specification, until the groan of yielding metal, the crack of the coupling, and the heavy thud of a worker collapsing onto a rebar grid filled her senses with chalk dust and copper blood. At forty-seven, an African American architect of twenty years, she could not deliberately summon the memory of the collapse without her mind slipping into a resistant fog; when fragments did surface, the metallic taste would flood her mouth, and the phantom screech of tearing steel would ring in her head, unbidden and persistent. These intrusions were not mere flashes; they were full-sensory reconstructions that hijacked her present. Because the memories constantly highlighted her own negligence, they naturally deepened her conviction that she was fundamentally flawed and uniquely vulnerable, pushing her further into isolation. Because she had come to believe that a competent professional would never have allowed the framing to fail, she actively walled off any attempt to revisit the site. The conviction that she was uniquely flawed hardened her resolve to keep the memory locked away, which effectively reinforced her inability to access the event when she tried. These appraisals of profound inadequacy and separation also compelled her to construct rigid psychological defenses. To manage the unrecognizable self she had become, Amara began performing mental rituals every time she touched a structural diagram, silently repeating load formulas to ward off further catastrophe. She told herself she was fortunate others had not been permanently disabled, and she would endlessly dwell on the precise millimeter where her judgment failed, convincing herself that the relentless dread was the only proof that she remained responsible for what happened. When the memory finally breached that barrier, it did not arrive quietly. The taste of dust and the phantom auditory recall instantly flooded her nervous system, convincing her body that the framework was collapsing again. Her heart would hammer against her ribs, and she would flinch violently whenever a nearby site dropped a tool or a heavy door slammed, reacting to ordinary office noise as if the danger were unfolding in real time. This constant state of hypervigilance and fractured attention made it impossible for her to navigate her architectural studio without exhaustion. The vivid sensory recall of the trauma directly triggered her need for control, pushing her to perform mental rituals and ruminate on her perceived errors to prevent recurrence. The sheer panic of the false alarms actually made it harder for her to process the original trauma, so she avoided the blueprints entirely, which in turn kept the memory fragmented and inaccessible. The more her nervous system fired false alarms and disrupted her focus, the more the unrecognizable person she had become seemed to replace her former self. The isolation felt absolute, as though she existed on a different frequency from her husband and colleagues, forever set apart by the weight of her error. These appraisals of profound inadequacy and separation naturally deepened the cognitive fog around the event, making the memory even more fragmented and inaccessible. Conversely, the relentless false alarms and concentration deficits constantly reminded her of her perceived fragility, reinforcing the belief that she was uniquely vulnerable. In the studio, her coping strategies became a cage. The downward comparisons and self-blame rumination made the site visits unbearable, so she stopped reviewing progress on the blueprints, a decision that ultimately sidelined her from lead projects. This constant rumination naturally fed back into her negative appraisals, convincing her that she was fundamentally broken and utterly alone. Simultaneously, the rituals heightened her alertness to environmental cues, which in turn kept the false alarms and concentration deficits firmly intact. The avoidance of the site itself left the sensory ghosts of dust and screaming metal entirely unprocessed, which prevented adaptive closure and kept the original trauma locked in isolation. It was this tightening loop that finally compelled her to seek help. Amara sat in the therapist’s office, her hands still trembling at the sound of the radiator clanking, hoping to break the cycle of dread. What frightened her most was that the rituals and comparisons were no longer containing the fear, only feeding it. She desperately wanted to reclaim the architect who once trusted her calculations, but she feared that without intervention, the unrecognizable self she had become would never recognize the woman she used to be.
